description: This is Team NoCoast, the best team from Chicago! Get ready to lock in and win this hackathon :D
summary: We built LunarNav, an intuitive, compact dashboard that lets users of all experience levels evaluate landing sites on the Moon's south pole. We developed this to address the problem that the current interfaces for comparing landing zones are clunky, dated, and difficult to use, even for experts, and they are completely inaccessible for those seeking to learn. To fix this, we centralized most of the information in one animated visual, showing exactly when a lander would contact mission control on Earth and when it would be getting power from direct sunlight over the course of a mission. We let users change the lander's parameters, including how long the stay will be, and directly compare locations in one easy-to-use panel. For more technical users, we let them pick any point on the south pole to test and provide additional statistics, such as optimal solar panel orientation and the effects of potential delays. This improved interface is important because it gives students a chance to learn the intricacies of landing a rover on the moon and become future mission analysts. For existing professionals, it will make their job more enjoyable and more efficient, which could be crucial if they need to make last-minute changes to mission planning.
details:
What our project does:

  • LunarNav is a web application that helps users compare landing sites near the Moon’s south pole at different dates. It estimates whether equipment will have enough solar power, battery storage, and communication with Earth during a selected stay.
  • We use NASA’s Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter elevation data to calculate the terrain horizon around a location. JPL’s DE421 ephemeris provides the positions of the Sun and Earth, which we compare with that horizon to predict visibility.
  • Our solar model calculates panel output using panel area, efficiency, orientation, and the Sun’s distance. A battery simulation then tracks how that energy supplies equipment, charges storage, and covers demand during darkness.
  • Users can compare six pre-programmed sites or explore custom coordinates they pick. Additional tools suggest landing dates, test delays, optimize panel orientations, estimate terrain steepness, and explore communication through a simulated satellite relay.

Main benefits:

  • LunarNav brings terrain, sunlight, power, and communication analysis into one workspace. Users can examine how these conditions interact when they change a location, date, or equipment setting.
  • The results explain why a mission meets or misses its requirements. Users can inspect electrical outages, unmet energy demand, landing difficulty, and the longest communication gaps instead of relying on a single overall score.
  • The application makes technical results easier to understand through plain-language explanations and synchronized visualizations. Detailed data and exports support users who want to examine the calculations more closely.

Intended impact: 

  • We want LunarNav to support early comparisons of lunar mission options. A mission planner could use it to identify promising site and date combinations before pursuing more detailed engineering analysis. Our project makes this significantly easier to do than with previous interfaces.
  • We also want students and public visitors to experiment with the decisions behind a lunar landing. Changing a landing date or battery size lets them see how an engineering choice affects the rest of a mission.
  • The project connects publicly available NASA data with questions people can investigate themselves, such as how a delayed landing changes power availability or how a relay satellite improves Earth contact.

Tools and software used:

  • We built the frontend with TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. Three.js handles the interactive 3D graphics, and Vite supports development and production builds.
  • Our Python backend uses FastAPI to serve analysis results, NumPy for numerical calculations, and Skyfield with JPL DE421 for astronomical positions.
  • We use Microsoft Azure Static Web Apps for the frontend and Azure Container Apps for the backend. We used GitHub to collaborate and GitHub actions to run automated checks on deployments.
  • LunarNav runs in a web browser. Its development centers on software, numerical models, and NASA terrain and astronomy datasets.

Creative aspects that help user understanding:

  • Users can move between a view from the landing site, a view above it, and the whole Moon within one 3D scene. This connects the scale of a local ridge with its consequences for a mission.
  • The timeline links the visual experience to the calculations. Seeing Earth disappear behind terrain helps explain why a communication gap occurs at that particular time.
  • Users can experiment with proposed solutions immediately. They can change panel orientation, increase storage, choose another date, or enable a simulated relay and compare the resulting mission conditions.

Main technical and other considerations:

  • We considered data quality and uncertainty. For example, for locations where we only had coarse terrain estimates we lower their resolution so users can visually tell how much detail there is.
  • We kept coordinate systems, units, and timestamps consistent across the terrain, astronomy, and power models. Those conventions matter because a mismatch can change the calculated visibility or energy.
  • We considered browser performance and backend workload. Adaptive terrain detail, caching, and limits on simultaneous requests help manage the calculations and graphics. Running the backend on Azure makes our website more reliable since the service is almost always running. This also makes LunarNav more accessible as anybody can run it so long as they have an internet connection.
  • We designed for people with different technical backgrounds through plain-language results and optional expert details. We also state model limits, including excluded thermal and dust effects, and distinguish preliminary slope screening from landing-safety assessment.
